prompt: At many universities, live lectures are being replaced by recorded material which students watch in their own time. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?
essay:
Recorded lectures have moved from being an emergency measure to being a permanent arrangement at many universities. I think the development is a positive one, but only because it exposes how little of a lecture ever needed to happen in a particular room at nine in the morning.

The advantages for students are substantial and mostly practical. A recording can be paused, replayed and watched at a speed that suits the listener, which matters enormously to anyone working in a second language or meeting an unfamiliar technical vocabulary for the first time. Students who commute, who work part time or who have caring responsibilities recover hours each week that were previously spent travelling in order to hear something they could have heard anywhere. Universities can also reach students who would not have been able to attend at all.

The losses are real but they are losses of a different kind. What disappears is not the content, which transmits perfectly well through a screen, but the incidental contact: the question asked afterwards, the conversation on the way out, the sense of belonging to a cohort rather than an audience. Attendance also becomes invisible, and students who were struggling used to be identifiable by their empty seats. These are serious, though they are arguments about what should replace the lecture rather than arguments for keeping it.

That is the condition on my answer. Recording lectures is a gain if the hours it frees are spent on seminars, supervision and the kind of contact that cannot be recorded. If it is simply a way of teaching more students with fewer staff, the same change becomes a straightforward reduction in what a degree contains.
title: Recorded material replacing the live lecture
